posts.content_md:
Most likely, you could do something similar to how DeFreitas does holoportraits:

[http://www.holoworld.com/holoportraits/](http://www.holoworld.com/holoportraits/)

This uses multiple source images which are sideways panning in perspective. To animate, just animate each image as well as altering it's perspective. You expose the transmission master (H1) in 'slits' to each of these images. Then, copy the H1 to create a reflection hologram (H2) with the image 'popping out'.

[http://www.3dimagery.com/mbreflct.html](http://www.3dimagery.com/mbreflct.html)

Beware, though, that the more you make an image pop-out from the film, the more distortion it could have. Here's a great paper on how to minimize the distortions (thanks to Kaveh!):

[http://www.holographer.org/articles/hg0 ... 00009.html](http://www.holographer.org/articles/hg00009/hg00009.html)

This takes a bit of equipment and a lot of time to get everything right. Just making a decent single Denisyuk reflection hologram for me has taken a lot of time. 

If you don't have a laser or any other gear like that yet, I would suggest you get a holokit from Integraf. That's what I've been working with thus far. You can at least get some basics down and get the mirrors and lenses later as you get more saphisticated.

Good luck! And, post pictures when you get something neat!

-Phil

posts.post_subject: (HELP)  How  to make  an hologram animated in the air?
posts.content_md:
What do you mean by "animated" and "standing in air"? You cannot have a free floating hologram of an object standing in air with no plate. You need to illuminate a plate somehow. You can disguise the plate, as a window or something, and have an object apparently freely hanging, but the plate still needs to be lit.

If by "animated" you mean that it moves, you need to move the hologram. It's possible to make this type of hologram by taking individual frames of a movie and making a "holographic video" out of them. These types are called either "multiplex" or "lenticular holograms" or "holo-odeons" or "integral holograms". This is one of the most famous: [http://www.physics.umd.edu/lecdem/servi ... /m6-12.htm](http://www.physics.umd.edu/lecdem/services/demos/demosm6/m6-12.htm)

The bottom of this page tells one way of making them:

[http://www.holo.com/holo/book/book5.html](http://www.holo.com/holo/book/book5.html)

Basically you project imndividual frams onto an LCD or with a movie projector. You then use optics to convert the image into a single thin slice and image the slice onto the holographic film. You move the holo film, slice the next frame and image that etc for all the frames.

Thanks for the link and the picture. I still think it's not possible to suspend particles in air and then image onto them. I have difficulty understanding how such particles stay in the air. In your case, you say the suspended particles were vaporised NaCl. But the melting point of NaCl is 800C and the boiling point considerably higher. How do you maintain these temperatures in a room full of people? Also, if this had been a holographic reconstruction with the hologram embedded in the projector, how could the entire audience see an image that far off image plane with zero dispersion? The light from the projector must have been a large thermal source which would mean that the image would also blur badly. Where was the H2? Another factor may be that if the image was truly 3D, there would have been massive parallax between the two ends of the planetarium. Each side would have seen a distorted gravity well, with only viewers in the center, directly below the projector, presumably, seeing an undistorted image. I suspect more likely the "hologram" was a HOE (somewhat like these pen lasers that image a flat picture on a wall). I suspect it was a Fourier Transform hologram of a 2D gravity well image drawn in perspective. This way, the entire audience would see the same image (no parallax) and there would have been no dispersion.

[quote:e663f006c9] Dinesh, is there (currently) any way to create a fluorescing point in open air[/quote:e663f006c9]

That's a possible scheme. Difficult, but I believe possible. You may have seen Tesla coil discharges, most science museums do a Tesla coil demo where huge electric arcs are sent across a room. if you could find a fluorescent material that could be crushed into small particles and if you could suspend the material within a volume and if you could persuade the arc to go through it, you may create fluorescnece. The suspension part is the most difficult. I don't see how you can suspend anything in air with some form of dispersion over time. However, it may j-u-u-u-st be possible to shoot these particles into the air suspend them locally just long enough for the spark to hit them and cause them to fluoresce for a very short time. I suspect the moment the spark hit them, the local temperature would shoot up, causing the local air density to fall and so cause the particles to (literally!) crash and burn. Fine particles are held up in air due to their large surface area compared to their mass. The arc would also have to discharge at just the right time before the particles dispersed. The surface area creates an Archimedian force up while gravity causes them to fall. This depends a lot on the local air density.

Now if you relaxed the "suspend in air" part and allow them to look as if they were supended in air, it becomes easier. Part of the demo is to take an ordinary fluoresent light bulb and watch it glow near the arc. If you could trap the gas in a (very, very clean!) glass shaped like, say a cat, it too would fluoresce nrear a Tesla coil and you'd see an apparent image of a cat in mid-space. Done against a dark background with the glass shape suspended by wire from above, the effect would be more dramatic. Sectioning off the glass shape and placing different gases in the various "compartments" of the glass shape would create an effect in colour.

Let me go over the parameters of the problem:

1. An image that remains static over a given volume of space and apparently not caused by any obvious visible agent. Any agent causing this image would have to have it's relative displacement be constant over the period of viewing.

2. This image exists in a volume of space that is not to be constrained by any obvious or visible means. 

3. The image is to be visible through some given theta such that:

0 <theta<360

4. The image apparently is not illuminated or does not exude from an agent (such as, for example, a nearby hoographic plate). In fact, the image seems to be a source of light itself.

4a. The image light is bright enough to be seen with the unaided eye under given circumstances (perhaps outdoors, perhaps indoors in a brightly lit room or perhaps only in a darkened room)

Have I covered the problem sufficently?

[quote:8f25c9aa11] Dinesh, have you never encountered dust? [/quote:8f25c9aa11]

By dust is presumably meant the minute particles that routinely float around in the atmosphere. The average diameter of such particles is approx 1 micron, or about 2*lambda for green light. At these diameters, I can think of no agent that would maintain the relative displacement of two dust particles. Dust floats as a result of it's relatively large surface area as a function of it's mass. Thus dust is very prone to slight modifications of local temperature, air currents. We may therefore conclude that mutual gravitation is too weak to overcome frictional forces to hold them at a fixed distance. What about electrostatic attraction? Well, there's a possibility. you'd need:

q_i(r_i)*q_j(r_j)/(|r_i^2 - r_j^2|) = k

Which would mean that the charges q_k would be very, very localised to overcome the myriad lofcal forces due to small changes in temperature, viscosity etc. I think this violates condition 1.

Insofar as I'm aware, dust cannot be self-illuminated. It can be illuminated by an external source, but this violates condition 4.

[quote:8f25c9aa11] Once a material is converted to a vapor state in open air, it doesn't necessarly require that the temperature remain the same to remain in the vapor state. Consider water, when you boil it and convert it to vapor, it doesn't immediately all condense back out around the pot. [/quote:8f25c9aa11]

A vapour state is defines as that state in which the kinetic energy of the molecules is large enough to overcome the Van der Waals forces between them. In order to give the molecules an amount of KE you need to give them energy,

E = 3/2kT

where k = Boltzmann's constant

and T = temperature. 

Once you cool them, T drops and so does E. If a vapour expnads into an area where the temperature is too low to maintain the vapour state, the KE of the molecules are transferred to the molecules of the surrounding environment. heat loss occurs as a result of convection and conduction. Eventually the steam cools off. However the vapour state remains not despite the loss of the heat source, but because of it. The KE of the water molecules is being transferred slowly into the air. Until all the molecules have lost their KE, the steam remains steam. Water is a funny animal because it's so highly polar.

[quote:8f25c9aa11]It's more likely that the localized concentration of cooling vapor resulted in a certain degree of solidified droplet formation, enough of which were small enough to remain suspended long enough for the display.[/quote:8f25c9aa11]

Again, what kept them from drifting apart and dispersing? Even assuming that the salt crystals solidified, too small and while viscosity and Archimedean forces would hold them up, they'd scatter and diffract so much the image would be very blurry. If the particles were large enough to not show diffraction effects, they'd be large enough to fall, since now mass is comparable to surface area. Blink, and you'll miss it!

[quote:8f25c9aa11] I assumed that this was essentially an H1[/quote:8f25c9aa11]

So the image was a pseudoscopic image from an H1? With no dispersion? Or at least, the most fantastic job of dispersion compensation I've ever seen!? Again, where was the H1. Sorry, Gary, I don't know you and so I have no way of knowing your level of knowledge. However, when you mention:

[quote:548f64c8d4] The material suspended in the air was vaporized salt[/quote:548f64c8d4]

I had to look twice. "Vaporized" to me has a specific scientific meaning. It means to raise the temperature of a substance such that it goes into a gaseous or vapour state. To suspend "vaporized salt", the temperature of the dome would have to be immense! When you went on to say that a substance can retain it's vapour state as the temp lowered and gave the example of water (steam) retaining it's vapour state after it left a hot pot, I figured I was talking to someone ignorant of basic Thermodynamics.

I must also apologise for another assumption (sometimes I answer these too quickly!). Since we were discussing "Princess Leia" holograms, I was assuming that you were stating that the gravity well was a Princess Leia hologram. The reason I was thinking of throwing in the towel was that I, too, was:

[quote:548f64c8d4] I too became sick to death of those people who weren't nearly so smart as they thought they were, who struggled through their copies of Omni magazine, and told me that it really was possible to produce those three dimensional people in the middle of the room with some silly projection unit like they saw on tv the night before.[/quote:548f64c8d4]

I know the ghosts are not holograms (they're actually underneath) and I call this the most famous non-hologram of all time. However, it's bad enough trying to convince Omni readers, but when holographers themselves try to convince me that Princess Leia holograms are possible, I wonder what the general public thinks. If holographers all stood together and said that some things are impossible (in present technology anyway) they might get a clearer idea of what holograms are. Instead you have the nothing-is-impossible crowd telling the public that Princess Leia hologramms are possible and then inventing fantastic and bizarre (and non-holographic) methods to justify the statement. Is it any wonder that the public at large believe the ghosts are holograms and that the HoloDeck is possible? It's bad enough that genuine holographers have to go through hoops trying to legitimise holography to the public, but when half the holographers (especially the "names" - another bee in my bonnet!) start trying to sell them Star Wars and Star Trek stuff, do you wonder the reputation holography has?

Anyway, Joy, who's an astronomer (or was at any rate) tells me that this was done by suspended, very fine particles that are constantly renewed. Apparently very fine particles are propelled by heat and suspend for a short time. These particles are constantly renewed and are too fine to be seen as such. The projection is done in the same way as a laser light show, ie it's scanned very rapidly in 3D space. So, in effect, it was the atomiser concept, but scanned rather than "holographically projected". The fact that I thought you implied it was a hologram surprised me. It could not have been the pseudo of an H1 or an image planed H2. The problem is that you can't just say "That's impossible". I try to explain the problems involved and time and time again I get the most incredible denial or twisting of the laws of physics.

[quote:548f64c8d4] I haven't spouted a "but they laughed at Galileo" but rather a "just because you don't know how it was done doesn't mean it wasn't done"[/quote:548f64c8d4]

True. However, when the person stipulates that it was done in a way you know it could not have been done, then I think you can say that while the effect itself is possible this particular effect was not done in that particular way. When I see a magician make something like a mountain or The Statue of Liberty disappear, I know that the thing itself doesn't really disappear. I can see the effect. However, if someone tried to convince me that I was actually seeing a life-sized Statue of Liberty hologram in true colour and it was actually the hologram that disappeared, I have to object! I don't know how the magician made the statue disappear, but I know that there is no way of making a hologram hundreds of feet high on a 4x5 plate and "projecting" this against the backdrop of the New York skyline ! I just accept the fact that it was an illusion that I don't understand, but that it was an illusion. As I said, "floating images" have been around for ages.

So, on to your problems:

[quote:548f64c8d4] 1. How to "project" the 3D or volumetric image. -We can already do this. [/quote:548f64c8d4]

Yes, we can do this already. I object to the word "project" since the holographic image is not "projected". The diffracted wavefront collapses into a volume of space. But that's splitting hairs Actaully, the raw beam experiment you mention with the bee is a projection phenomena, which is why it was so huge. A holographic image will not expand as you move a "viewing screen" further away, but the (2D) image of a hologram reconstructed with a raw beam and projected onto a screen will expand as you move the screen back.

[quote:548f64c8d4] 2. How to make it bigger then the originating plate, and farther away than the original object.- Anyone? Is there an optical solution to this? (violation of physical laws will be punished severely)[/quote:548f64c8d4]

By altering the beam divergence of the reconstruction beam relative to the reference beam. You can get an especially dramatic effect by making the hologram with a converging ref and then using a very, very divergent beam to reconstruct it. Effectively you get barrell or pincushion distortion which will give the appearance of making the image larger and further away. Of course, it will also distort the object a lot. This: [http://4c-s.org/v-web/gallery/albums/al ... oyl_19.jpg](http://4c-s.org/v-web/gallery/albums/album02/Gargoyl_19.jpg) was made to be reconstructed with a highly divergent recon beam. When seen with a collimating recon, it's pretty smalle and off image plane. However, if you're talking as large as the gravity well, then as I said, that was a scanning technique. It's j-u-u-st possible by making a very, very small, relatively flat object very very close to the plate with a very, very convcerging beam. Then reconstructing with a very, very divergent beam. But personally I doubt even that will work for the dimensions of a large hall.

[quote:548f64c8d4] 3. Find a suitable projection material, one that can be suspended in the air for at least a short period. -Whitish salt microspheres? Smoke? Water mist? Flour? Titanium Dioxide? Tiny faeries? [/quote:548f64c8d4]

Can the faieries be put through a blender? Jeff mentions Ammonium Chloride. The effect you showed (gravity well) was apparently done with a fine mist, so Joy who's seen it, tells me. In fact I'mm being told it's a common part of laser light shows but using smoke. I suppose anything that wind tunnel people use will do. In some cases, such as the gravity well effect, the substance needs to be renewed.

[quote:548f64c8d4] 4. Properly illuminate the originating plate with enough light to produce the desired effect without incinerating the plate. (Agh! My eye! Am I on fire!?) [/quote:548f64c8d4]

Assuming it can be done, and it sort of can on a much smaller scale that a large auditorium, then the reflective properties of the suspension is the deciding factor on the viewability, especially in a dark room. Without actually calculating it (no time, I have to get to the studio! I have students coming in an hour!) I'd imagine that the de of the hologram can be a reasonable 25%-40% and illuminated with a 1W diverging beam provided the albedo of the suspended particles is sfficently high.

[quote:548f64c8d4] Dinesh, if you've read this far, please note that I sympathize, and please remember that things have been done that we didn't figure out.[/quote:548f64c8d4]

Thanks. Of course things have been done that I haven't figured out. But, as you say, there are ways it could not have been done. If someone proposes that the effect is created by breaking the known laws of physics, I say so. Usually I then get, "But we don't know all the laws of Physics" or "You scientists think you know everything" (usually I say, "No, we don't know everything, but I'm willing to bet I know anything you might want to know")

[quote:ab8ade55e0] But, recall that original question, an "animated hologram standing in air"

Well, as I see it, therer are three types of impossibility:

1. Things that really are impossible

2. Things that are impossible given our level of knowledge and/or ability

3. Things that are impossible because we cannot concieve of them.

I think 1 and 2 are related in that they're both articles of faith - call 1 a 'strong article of faith' and 2 a 'weak article of faith'. Examples of 1 are that it's impossible to braeth in a vacuum (unaided). Examples of 2 is that it's impossible to go faster than the spedd of light and 3 might be the famous ones (can't fly with a heavier-than-air craft etc). Maybe 1 an3 are also related somehow, since things that are really impssible are so because I can't concieve of them. However, I still believe some things are really impossible, otherwise Laws of Nature make no sense. The Laws must exist to give a framework of possible results of experiments. I'd say that the animated hologram in air is of type 2. I can concieve of a few ways of doing this, but I believe it's beyond our present technology. I think that one day it'll be done, but not today. This is assuming we're talking specifically of a hologram and not just any means of suspending an image in apparent free space (albeit with suspendid stuff in the air) and that animation is also caused holographically, such as in a multiplex. It can be done on a small scale, though. The atomiser concept with a roll of holo film, each one recorded with a different frame of video can do this. Stick the roll of holo film recorded with subsequent frames in laser transmission format on the outside of a clear box, puff talcum powder or something into the box. There are fancier ways involving pumping non-linear liquids using an electrical ly induced birefringent effect - put this liquid in the box, zap it and birefringemnce makes it cloudy. Coordinate the zaps with the frame rate. Throw a low power laser (we wouldn't want anyone hurting themselves ) at the film and advance the film. Viewer will see an apparent holographic movie inside the clear box.

You should see some of the early stuff that came out of those minds! I was once asked if anything truly new, with no derivation at all from anything previous to it, existed.  "Hollapse", that's not bad. "Subfuse"? -like a sort of opposite of diffuse? I found it interesting that much of what he did seemed to have been fueled by having been (figuratively) screwed by Edison early on.

 There is one thing...

 Any idea how that worked? More importantly, how to make one and how to "tune" it? If we could power so much as a flashlight with such a thing, we'd have that billion-dollar item.

 Faster Than Light. Light beer?

 Grand Unified Field Theory. Wasn't that an attempt to standardize baseball playing venues?

 Cancer. I had it, and now I'm listed as "cured". That was Big Fun. =8P (no suitable emoticon)

 Perpetual motion. I know people who ask for money, and the less you give them the more they ask for it. It appears there's more energy coming out than going in, but I'm quite sure it's being piped in from elsewhere.

 I read something about an 1800's patent for making diamonds. In essence:

 Start with a pressure vessel. Insert Sodium and Carbon. You'll need an inert atmosphere for the sodium. Apply heat to melt the sodium, which will then dissolve the carbon (?).
